meta.title: GymPro · Training log with an AI coach
meta.description: Plan routines, log every set, and ask Ronnie, an AI coach that checks your actual workouts before it answers. In English and Traditional Chinese.

hero.title: A training log with a coach who reads it.
hero.body: Plan your routines, log every set, and ask Ronnie, GymPro's AI coach, whenever you're not sure what to do next. Ronnie looks at what you've actually trained before answering, and can adjust today's workout for you.

chat.label: Example chat: Ronnie suggests a substitute, and today's workout changes only when you tap Swap.
chat.subtitle: AI Personal Coach
chat.user: My lower back is tight today. Can I swap squats for something easier on it?
chat.reply: I'd swap Barbell Back Squat for Leg Press today: it's easier on your lower back. Go lighter than usual, and stop if it starts to hurt.
chat.swapped: ✓ Swapped "Barbell Back Squat" for "Leg Press" today

how.title: Plan, log, ask, review
how.intro: Four parts that feed each other: the more you log, the more Ronnie and your reports have to work with.

plan.title: Build routines and a cycle
plan.body: Pick exercises from the built-in library, set sets and reps, and arrange routines into a cycle of any length, rest days included. Or answer a few questions and let Coach G draft routines and a cycle for you to review before saving.

log.title: Log every set
log.body: The Today card opens on the day's routine from your cycle. Enter reps and weight as you go, in kg or lb, and add or drop exercises when plans change.

ask.title: Ask Ronnie
ask.body: Ronnie checks your workouts and routines before answering. It can add or swap exercises in today's workout, find an exercise from a description in English or Chinese, and suggest routine changes that only apply once you confirm.

review.title: Get a report every period
review.body: When a period ends (a week, or one full cycle), an AI Coach Report is written for you: training split, strength trend, progressive overload and what to do next, taking your notes for the period into account. History keeps past periods and your weight trend.

researchText.lift_stalled: In an 8-week study of leg training in people with a year or more of lifting, adding reps at the same weight built muscle and strength about as well as adding weight. So GymPro suggests adding reps first, then weight once every set reaches the top of the range (double progression).
researchText.lift_regressed: A short dip can be fatigue that recovery reverses; a drop that lasts is the warning sign of overtraining. So GymPro suggests holding the weight and looking after recovery, rather than adding load or stopping.
researchText.deload: Deload weeks rest mostly on coaches' experience, with few trials; in one study, a scheduled week off midway made no difference to muscle growth but led to smaller strength gains. In a survey of 246 strength and physique athletes, a deload lasted about a week, mainly to manage fatigue, with the same days and exercises, fewer sets and lighter weights. So GymPro doesn't schedule deloads: it suggests a lighter week, not a week off, when several main lifts drop together, or when you say you're tired and your lifts drop; about 10% lighter with half the sets is GymPro's setting.
researchText.low_volume: The largest meta-analysis (67 studies) found that about 4 sets a week already give measurable growth, and more sets keep adding muscle, each a little less. Up to 10, about 6 more sets give one more measurable step (about 2%, the smallest difference studies detect); past 10 it takes 8 or more, and more the higher you go. So GymPro suggests more sets below 10 when the muscle bears on your goal, where each set buys the most growth; adding 1-2 sets a week at a time is a gradual step, not a number from the studies.
researchText.missed_sessions: With total sets equal, how often you train barely changes growth but helps strength; what a missed session really costs is that week's sets. So GymPro suggests fitting the missed routines in, not swapping in other exercises. When fewer than 3 in 4 planned sessions get done two weeks running, with no illness or travel said, it suggests a smaller plan you can keep instead, with nothing added; 3 in 4 is GymPro's threshold.
researchText.weight_trend: For a cut before a competition, losing 0.5–1% of body weight a week is advised to keep the most muscle; a modest surplus helps a bulk, but how much is unsettled. So GymPro suggests a small change in calories, not a crash diet.
researchText.cardio_first: Two meta-analyses found that lifting before cardio in the same session gave more lower-body strength (about 4 kg more on the 1RM), with no difference in muscle growth; a newer umbrella review saw the same trend, short of significance. So when cardio comes before the leg lifts on a leg day, GymPro suggests lifting first and doing the cardio after, or at another time.
researchText.goal_path: Add reps the way you train now, then the smallest weight step once every set reaches the top; each other way has research behind it, listed below.
researchText.next_session: A study found that adding reps at the same weight grew muscle and strength about as well as adding weight; the American College of Sports Medicine suggests 2-10% more weight once you can do 1-2 reps more than the set calls for. So GymPro adds reps first, then the smallest step once every set reaches the top.
researchText.pain_hold: No more weight on what hurts; if it lasts more than a week, have a doctor or physical therapist look at it. This is a safety rule, not a study's finding.
researchText.few_days: WHO's 2020 guidelines suggest adults do muscle-strengthening activities that work the major muscle groups on 2 or more days a week. A meta-analysis of 16 cohort studies linked muscle-strengthening to a 10–17% lower risk of early death, heart disease, cancer and diabetes, the most at about 30–60 minutes a week. So when you train on fewer than 2 days a week, GymPro suggests 2.

cardio.researchText: Meta-analyses found that adding cardio to lifting builds muscle and maximal strength about as well as lifting alone, with better aerobic fitness; explosive strength is what can be blunted, more so in the same session. So GymPro only records your cardio and never asks for more or less of it; its one note is to lift first on leg days.
cardio.who: WHO suggests 150–300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week for adults, or 75–150 of vigorous, or a mix in which a vigorous minute counts as two; everyday activity like walking to work counts too, and this counts only what you logged.
cardio.equivalent: Counted as WHO does, a vigorous minute as two: about {n} min a week.
cardio.unrated: {n} min have no heart rate and aren't rated.
cardio.maxHr: Your maximum heart rate is estimated at {n} bpm from your age.
cardio.needsAge: Some sets have a heart rate. Add your birth date in <link>Settings</link> to rate them.
cardio.intensityText: ACSM rates aerobic intensity by the share of maximum heart rate: 64–76% is moderate and 77–95% vigorous; below 64% is light. GymPro estimates the maximum from your age as 208 − 0.7 × age, the equation a meta-analysis of 351 studies found, the same for men and women. It is an estimate, not a measurement, so the rating is a guide; a set without a heart rate isn't rated.
cardio.trendTitle: Same setting, heart rate over time
cardio.trendText: A review of heart-rate monitoring found that heart rate at the same submaximal work marks fitness: the lower it is, the fitter, and its fall goes with better endurance performance. It also varies from day to day, so a trend over several sessions says more than one. Only sets of 10 minutes or more are compared.

ruleText.cardio_first: 15 minutes or more of cardio before the first leg lift in the same session; a 5–10 minute warm-up doesn't count (the order is when each set was logged)
ruleText.goal_path: A lift your goal names: the next session the way you train it now, and other ways research supports
ruleText.next_session: Your other main lifts: reach the top reps on every set, then add weight
ruleText.pain_hold: A lift you said hurt this {unit, select, week {week} other {cycle}}, or one that loads the sore joint more than lightly

e1rm.text: A one-rep max estimated from weight and reps (Epley), so 80 kg × 10 and 85 kg × 6 can be compared.

record.text: A main lift's best set this {unit, select, week {week} other {cycle}} beat every earlier set.

weeklySets.text: Sets logged for each muscle, scaled to a week. A muscle an exercise mainly trains counts a full set, one it trains on the side counts half, the counting that fit the research best of those a meta-analysis compared. Shoulders are split into front, side and rear delts, and legs into quads and hamstrings, because different movements train them.

status.text: More main lifts up than down is progressing; the reverse is slipping; equal is holding steady.

planResearch.progress: A study found that adding reps at the same weight grew muscle and strength about as well as adding weight; the American College of Sports Medicine suggests 2-10% more weight once you can do 1-2 reps more than the set calls for. So GymPro adds reps first, then the smallest step once every set reaches the top.
planResearch.heavy: A network meta-analysis comparing ways to train found heavier loads (above about 80% of 1RM) ranked best for maximal strength. So a strength goal gets a "heavy first" option.
planResearch.frequency: The American College of Sports Medicine suggests training each muscle group two or more days a week for strength; a meta-analysis found more frequent training gave more strength, mostly through the extra sets. So a goal lift trained once a week gets a "second day" option.
planResearch.pullUp: A study found men's maximal lat pulldown was about 75-80% of their maximal pull-up. So GymPro uses the pulldown to estimate how far a first pull-up is; the checkpoint (80% of body weight) is GymPro's reading of that ratio, not a number the study gives.
